episode.broadcastScript:
This is The Innovation Pulse for the week ending Friday, May twenty-ninth, twenty twenty-six. And here's who is innovating in higher education this week.

<break time="1.0s"/>

This week's lead story comes from UC Berkeley, where a newly published study of more than ninety-five thousand undergraduates at twenty major U.S. public research universities found that two-thirds used generative A.I. during the twenty twenty-three to twenty twenty-four academic year. According to University of California news, regular use was highest among computer science students at sixty-two percent, followed by math at fifty-three percent and business at fifty-one percent. The research, published May twenty-first in Science by UC Berkeley's Center for Studies in Higher Education with collaborators from the University of Technology Sydney and Cornell University, also found that approximately nine percent of A.I. users reported using it to cheat on assignments. Among daily users, that rate rose to twenty-six percent. Cheating rates varied by discipline, with economics students at seventeen percent and journalism at sixteen percent, compared to five percent in biology. Lead researcher Igor Chirikov warned that A.I. undermines the informational value of academic assessment when students use it on assignments, causing grades to become inflated relative to actual knowledge. The paper argues that universities should develop discipline-specific policies and new ways of measuring students' knowledge and abilities that cannot be replicated with A.I., rather than implementing blanket bans. Non-STEM students cheated at higher rates than STEM students. The study also found that low-income, racially underrepresented, and female students used A.I. less frequently than their peers, creating potential career disadvantages as A.I. proficiency becomes increasingly important in the workforce.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Insights and Trends this week, roughly sixty-five percent of students and fifty-nine percent of faculty at California State University said they were skeptical that A.I. benefits education overall, according to a system-wide survey of more than ninety-four thousand respondents. NPR reported the findings as C.S.U., the largest public four-year system in the country with four hundred seventy thousand students, renews its thirteen million dollar annual contract with OpenAI for ChatGPT Edu. Despite the skepticism, eighty-four percent of students reported using ChatGPT, yet eighty percent said they would not be comfortable turning in A.I.-generated work as their own. Large majorities of respondents worry about A.I.'s impact on creativity, job security and the environment. The survey did not ask whether respondents agreed with the system's decision to spend millions on the OpenAI contract.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Ethical A.I. this week, the Illinois House passed a bill requiring the largest A.I. companies to publish safety plans and undergo independent third-party audits, making Illinois the third state to regulate frontier A.I. models. According to Capitol News Illinois, S.B. 315 passed the House one hundred ten to zero after the Senate approved it fifty-two to five. The bill targets companies with more than five hundred million dollars in revenue developing the most capable A.I. models. It takes effect January first, twenty twenty-seven, with audit requirements beginning January first, twenty twenty-eight. The bill creates whistleblower protections for A.I. company employees. OpenAI and Anthropic have publicly supported the measure, while the trade group TechNet has opposed it. Governor J.B. Pritzker has indicated he will sign it, writing on X that Illinois is leading the nation in holding Big Tech accountable.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Research this week, researchers at M.D. Anderson Cancer Center developed an A.I.-powered spatial atlas of tertiary lymphoid structures across multiple cancer types, published in Science. Led by Linghua Wang, the team created scalable A.I. frameworks to detect, profile and classify the structures from spatial genomics data and routine pathology slides. The research revealed how these specialized immune formations vary by tumor type and influence patient outcomes. The findings may help identify new therapeutic strategies to enhance the body's anti-tumor immune responses in cancer patients.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Also in Research, Penn State researchers demonstrated that A.I. can generate nearly four hundred complete, publication-ready finance research papers in roughly twelve hours using large language models. Associate Professor Mihail Velikov and University of Rochester's Robert Novy-Marx built an automated pipeline that produced papers nearly indistinguishable from human-authored research, according to findings published in the Journal of Economic Literature. Each A.I.-generated paper included abstracts, introductions, data analysis, results, conclusions and citations. The study raises concerns about the peer-review system and academic integrity.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In A.I. Workforce and Careers this week, a Stanford-led study analyzing more than four million job applications across one hundred fifty-six employers found that A.I. hiring tools showed clear racial disparities. According to Fortune, more than twenty-five percent of Black applicant submissions went to positions with discriminatory outcomes. The research, presented at the A.C.M. Conference on Fairness, Accountability, and Transparency, documented what researchers called an algorithmic blackball effect, where applicants using the same vendor faced correlated rejections across employers. Among those applying to ten positions, four percent were rejected universally, a rate higher than independent decision-making would predict. Researchers called for measuring adverse impact at the individual position level.

<break time="1.0s"/>

In Beyond Ed this week, Anthropic released Claude Opus four point eight, an upgraded version of its flagship A.I. model that the company says delivers better performance across coding, reasoning and knowledge work tasks. The model includes user control over effort levels and workflow features for large-scale programming projects, according to the company. The company says the model is around four times less likely than its predecessor to allow flaws in code to pass unremarked. Fast mode for the new model is three times cheaper than previous versions, the company says. Pricing for regular usage remains at five dollars per million input tokens and twenty-five dollars per million output tokens.

<break time="1.0s"/>

Finally in Beyond Ed, an OpenAI reasoning model produced a proof disproving a conjecture about geometry that mathematician Paul Erdős posed in nineteen forty-six, the company announced. The unit distance problem asks how many pairs of points placed on a plane can be exactly one unit apart. For nearly eight decades, mathematicians believed square grids were essentially optimal. OpenAI says its model found a configuration using higher-dimensional lattice theory that surpasses the long-standing record. Mathematicians consulted by OpenAI, including Fields Medalist Timothy Gowers and Daniel Litt of the University of Toronto, called the result legitimate, though they noted humans played a vital role in verifying and cleaning up the proof. The result has not yet undergone formal peer review.

<break time="1.0s"/>

That's this week's Innovation Pulse. Full coverage and source links at innovating higher ed dot com.

leadStory.headline: UC Berkeley Study of 95,000 Undergraduates Finds Two-Thirds Used A.I., Calls for Assessment Reform

The research, published May 21 in Science by UC Berkeley's Center for Studies in Higher Education with collaborators from the University of Technology Sydney and Cornell University, also found that approximately 9 percent of A.I. users reported using it to cheat on assignments. Among daily users, that rate rose to 26 percent. Cheating rates varied by discipline, with economics students at 17 percent and journalism at 16 percent, compared to 5 percent in biology. Lead researcher Igor Chirikov warned that A.I. undermines the informational value of academic assessment when students use it on assignments, causing grades to become inflated relative to actual knowledge. The paper argues that universities should develop discipline-specific policies and new ways of measuring students' knowledge and abilities that cannot be replicated with A.I., rather than implementing blanket bans. Non-STEM students cheated at higher rates than STEM students, and low-income, racially underrepresented, and female students used A.I. less frequently than peers, creating potential career disadvantages.
